questions.q: What is the determinant of A = [[2,1],[1,1]]?
Given A = [[2,1],[1,1]] with det(A) = 1, what is A inverse?
questions.explain: Swap the diagonal entries (2 and 1 become 1 and 2), negate the off-diagonal entries (both 1's become -1), then divide by det=1, giving [[1,-1],[-1,2]].

questions.q: Multiplying A = [[2,1],[1,1]] by the inverse found in this lesson, A^-1 = [[1,-1],[-1,2]], what should the product AA^-1 equal, and does it?
options: The identity matrix [[1,0],[0,1]], and the lesson's row-by-column computation confirms it
It cannot be computed because A and A^-1 have mismatched dimensions
questions.explain: Multiplying out AA^-1 entry by entry gives [[1,0],[0,1]] = I, which is exactly the defining property of an inverse: it undoes A's transformation completely.

questions.q: Why does a matrix with determinant zero have no inverse?
options: Because mathematicians have simply not yet discovered a formula for that case
Because all 2x2 matrices automatically have a nonzero determinant
It does have an inverse, just not one expressible with the ad-bc formula

The inverse formula requires dividing by the determinant, which is undefined at zero, and geometrically a zero determinant means the matrix collapses the plane so that information needed to reverse the transformation is genuinely lost
questions.explain: A zero determinant means the inverse formula divides by zero, and geometrically it means the transformation squashes distinct inputs to the same output, so there's no way to recover the original input -- no inverse can exist.

questions.q: Why must every valid quantum gate matrix be invertible?
options: Because invertible matrices are easier for computers to store in memory
Because only invertible matrices can be multiplied by vectors at all
Reversibility is not actually required for quantum gates, only for classical logic gates

Because quantum computation (apart from measurement) is reversible -- no information is ever destroyed, so it must always be possible to recover the input state from the output state, which requires a nonzero determinant
questions.explain: Quantum evolution never destroys information, so every gate must be undoable -- which is precisely the mathematical requirement that its matrix have a nonzero determinant and therefore an inverse.
